props.title: The Five Pennies
props.initialSlug: Horn legend Red Nichols' bittersweet music journey

sections.content: **The Five Pennies** (1959) stands as one of Hollywood's most compelling yet overlooked jazz biopics, with Danny Kaye delivering a career-defining performance as cornet player Red Nichols. Unlike the sanitized musician stories of its era, this film dares to show both the exhilarating highs of the 1920s jazz scene and the crushing personal costs of life on the road. It shares DNA with later jazz films like **Round Midnight** (1986) and **Bird** (1988) in its unflinching look at how music can both save and destroy its most devoted practitioners.

sections.content: The film's musical numbers, particularly the collaborations between Kaye and Louis Armstrong, capture the electric spontaneity of live jazz performance in ways that wouldn't be matched until **Whiplash** (2014). Director Melville Shavelson makes the innovative choice to let full songs play out rather than cutting them into montages, a technique that influenced later music films like **Ray** (2004) and **Get On Up** (2014).

What sets **The Five Pennies** apart is its focus on the family drama behind the music. The relationship between Nichols and his daughter Dorothy (Susan Gordon) provides emotional weight rarely seen in 1950s musician biopics. This approach influenced later films like **Coal Miner's Daughter** (1980) and **Walk the Line** (2005), which similarly balanced musical achievement with personal relationships. sections.content: The film's technical innovations in recording live performance laid groundwork for future music films. The way **The Five Pennies** captures the interplay between musicians influenced everything from **Round Midnight** (1986) to **Mo' Better Blues** (1990). Its pioneering sound mixing techniques, which allowed viewers to hear individual instruments within the full band context, created a template still used in contemporary music films like **Bohemian Rhapsody** (2018).
